passage:
Class 4 note, written by Pooja (class teacher).
On Tuesday, Varun read "photosynthesis" aloud as "photo-sin-thesis" and the class burst out laughing. Someone repeated it in the corridor and by Wednesday three children were calling him "Photo-sin". Varun laughed each time and even did a small bow.
But I noticed that he stopped putting up his hand in science, ate his tiffin alone and kept his eyes on his bag. Smiling isn't always the same as fine.
That afternoon I kept him back and said quietly, "I saw the laughing. It wasn't fair, and it isn't your fault." I spoke to the class about laughing with someone and laughing at them. Varun's mother is coming in on Friday, and I will check in with him next week.

qa.q: What nickname did three children call Varun by Wednesday?
qa.a: They called him "Photo-sin" by Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling behind his smile and bow?
qa.a: Varun was hurt and ashamed, shrinking inside. He stopped raising his hand, ate alone and looked at his bag.

qa.q: What did Pooja do the same day that helped Varun?
qa.a: Pooja spoke to him quietly, said it was not fair or his fault, and spoke to the class about laughing with and laughing at someone.

qa.q: How might the classmates who called him Photo-sin have seen it?
qa.a: They may have seen it as a joke, because Varun laughed and bowed. They may not have realised how it hurt.

grounding: A child whose mistake becomes the class joke smiles outwardly while shrinking inside; the smile is a survival tactic.

passage:
Thursday, after school.
Dear diary, today in English Miss asked me to read "hippopotamus" and I said "hippo-pot-a-muss." Everyone laughed. Even Miss smiled. I laughed too. I said, "Yes, yes, it's a big muss!" and that made them laugh harder. I did the funny voice on purpose so it would look like I meant it.
Tenzin didn't laugh. He just looked at his book. At break, some kids said "muss, muss" whenever I walked by, and I laughed each time. My cheeks hurt from smiling.
I kept my head down all afternoon. At home I told Mummy I had a stomach ache. I don't want to go tomorrow. I hope nobody remembers by then.
— Binita

qa.q: Which word did Binita say wrongly in English class?
qa.a: Binita said "hippopotamus" wrongly, reading it as "hippo-pot-a-muss."

qa.q: Why did Binita laugh along and do the funny voice?
qa.a: Binita felt embarrassed and wanted it to look as if it was meant. Laughing along was a way to get through the moment, though inside Binita was hurting.

qa.q: What could Binita do tomorrow so that Binita is not alone with this?
qa.a: Binita could tell Mummy or Miss what happened and how it felt. Binita could also sit near Tenzin, who did not laugh.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have been thinking when he looked at his book and did not laugh?
qa.a: Tenzin may have felt uncomfortable or sorry for Binita and did not want to join in. Looking away could have been his way of not adding to it.

grounding: A child whose mistake becomes a class joke laughs along outwardly while feeling small inside.

passage: In the Class 5 maths period at Ramakrishna Vidyalaya, Indu put up her hand and said, "Mummy, can I go to the toilet?" to Mrs. Nair. The room exploded. Kids banged desks. Someone shouted "Mummy!" in a baby voice. Indu laughed too, loud, and did a little bow. For the rest of the day, every time she walked past, somebody said "Mummy" and she smiled and waved like a film star. At lunch she ate half her tiffin and put the lid back on. Jahnavi, her deskmate, noticed her hands were shaking. After the bell, Mrs. Nair called Indu over quietly. "I saw that smile, and I saw your face at lunch. It's okay if it hurt." Indu's eyes filled up. Mrs. Nair spoke to the class the next morning, and told Indu's mother at pickup that day.

qa.q: What did Indu call Mrs. Nair by mistake?
qa.a: She called her 'Mummy'.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling while she smiled and waved like a film star?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and hurt inside, shrinking behind a laugh that protected her, as her shaking hands and half-eaten tiffin showed.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Nair help Indu, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She noticed the gap between Indu's smile and her face, spoke to her privately that same day, addressed the class and told Indu's mother at pickup.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi see Indu that day?
qa.a: Jahnavi noticed her shaking hands, so she saw that Indu's laughing along was not the whole story.

grounding: Shows a child whose slip becomes the class joke smiling outwardly while hurting inside, laughing along to survive.

passage:
"How was the match, Aadhya?"
"Fine, Uma Masi." Aadhya kicked off her shoes.
"Fine? You were so excited this morning."
"I dropped a really easy catch. Everyone laughed. Now they're calling me Butterfingers."
"Oh, beta."
"It's okay! It's actually funny. I laughed too." Aadhya grinned too wide.
Uma Masi put down the vegetables. "Did it feel funny?"
Aadhya's grin wobbled. "They kept saying it. Even Coach laughed a bit. I just kept laughing so they wouldn't see."
"So they wouldn't see what?"
"That I wanted to cry."
Uma Masi pulled her close. "Laughing along to get through it is clever. But it doesn't mean the joke was okay."
"Don't tell Coach."
"I'll call your mother now, and we'll decide together whether to talk to Coach. You won't be on your own with this."

qa.q: What were they calling Aadhya after the match?
qa.a: Butterfingers.

qa.q: What does Aadhya's too-wide grin suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Aadhya was hurt and embarrassed underneath, laughing along so others wouldn't see that she wanted to cry.

qa.q: How did Uma Masi support Aadhya well?
qa.a: She stopped what she was doing, asked gently whether it felt funny, named that laughing along didn't make the joke okay, and called Aadhya's mother right away.

qa.q: How might the teammates have seen Aadhya's laughing?
qa.a: They probably thought she found the nickname funny too, so they didn't realise it was hurting her.

grounding: Shows a child laughing along with a nickname after a mistake while hurting inside, and an adult seeing through it.

passage:
In Class 6 I leaned back on my chair during Hindi, and it slid out from under me. I landed flat, legs in the air. Raghav yelled, "Crash landing!" and the whole class roared.
I laughed louder than anyone, like I didn't care.
But all day, "crash landing" followed me. At lunch Raghav fell off the bench on purpose. I laughed again. My stomach felt tight, like a fist.
In the car I told Papa it was a funny day, then started crying. He pulled over and listened. He said laughing along had been my way of surviving, not proof the teasing was harmless. That evening he emailed my class teacher, and the next day she spoke to Raghav.
I'm Parul. I still laugh at stuff, but now I notice when my stomach is tight.

qa.q: What did Raghav yell when the narrator fell?
qa.a: He yelled, 'Crash landing!'

qa.q: How was Parul feeling while laughing at lunch?
qa.a: Parul felt hurt and tense inside, with a stomach tight like a fist, while laughing on the outside.

qa.q: What did Papa do that helped the same day?
qa.a: He pulled over, listened, told Parul that laughing along was surviving, not proof the teasing was harmless, and emailed the class teacher that evening.

qa.q: How might Raghav have seen the joke?
qa.a: Raghav probably thought Parul found it funny too, because Parul laughed loudest, so he kept repeating it.

grounding: Shows a child laughing along with a class joke about a mistake while shrinking inside, and an adult recognising it as a survival tactic.

passage:
Class 5A, teacher's note, Monday.
During reading aloud, Kashish read "the chef cooked a meal" as "the chief cooked a meal" and the class laughed. Jatin started calling "Chief! Chief!" By lunch it was a chant. Kashish laughed along every time, and once even bowed. But I noticed that Kashish ate lunch alone, didn't raise a hand, and kept pulling a sleeve down over the knuckles. When I asked quietly, "Is the chief joke okay with you?", Kashish said, "It's fine, it's funny," and then Kashish's eyes filled. I said it is okay not to find it funny. After lunch I spoke to Jatin separately; he said he thought Kashish liked it because of all the smiling. The nickname stops today, and I phoned home this evening.

qa.q: What word did Kashish read instead of "chef"?
qa.a: Kashish read "chief".

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling while laughing along with the chant?
qa.a: Kashish felt hurt and embarrassed inside, eating alone and pulling a sleeve over the knuckles, even while smiling and bowing.

qa.q: What could Jatin do now that he knows?
qa.a: He could drop the nickname and say sorry to Kashish, since he had taken the smiling to mean Kashish liked it.

qa.q: Why might Jatin have believed Kashish liked the joke?
qa.a: Because Kashish kept smiling and even bowed, so from outside, laughing along looked like enjoying it.

grounding: Shows a child whose reading slip becomes a class nickname laughing along on the outside while shrinking inside.
